title: Switzerland's Glaciers Lost 5.5% of Their Ice This Year — and They May Not Survive
summary:
Switzerland's glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate. This year alone, they lost 5.5% of their total ice volume — the second-largest annual decline ever recorded. Over the past five years, the country's glaciers have shrunk by nearly a fifth, according to the GLAMOS glacier monitoring service and the Swiss Academy of Sciences.

"Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions," the experts said in a statement.

The cause is clear: heat waves and low winter snowfall, driven by climate change. "The warming that we are experiencing now can be attributed 100 per cent to anthropogenic climate change. It's as simple as that," said Matthias Huss, who heads GLAMOS. "Without human emissions or fossil fuels we wouldn't have any warming at the moment."

Snow matters for two reasons, Huss explained. "On the one hand, it protects the bare ice from melting. The longer you have snow, the longer you avoid the loss of old ice," he said. "On the other hand, the snow is important also for generating new food for the glacier. The more snow you have, the higher the potential to keep some of the snow at high elevation and to form new ice."

The impact is huge. From July to September, Switzerland lost 2.2 trillion liters of water — four times the annual water consumption of the country's 9.1 million people. The average thickness of individual glaciers dropped by 2.5 to 4 meters, with some glacier tongues losing up to 10 meters. The Allalin, Clarident, Rhone, and Aletsch glaciers — Aletsch being the largest in the Alps — all experienced their biggest melt on record.

Switzerland is often called the "water tower of Europe" because its glaciers feed major rivers like the Danube, Po, Rhine, and Rhone. More than half of Switzerland's electricity comes from hydropower, which depends on glacier-fed water.

The record retreat was in 2022, when summer heat, low snowfall, and reddish dust from the Sahara darkened the ice and made it absorb more heat. This year's percentage loss was greater than in 2003 because the total ice volume is now roughly a third of what it was then.

Huss said there's still time to protect polar ice sheets. "For the ice in the polar regions like the ice sheets, there it's not yet too late," he said. "There, we can make a difference and we need to make a difference in order to limit sea level rise."
why_it_matters: Glacier melt in one small country is a preview of a worldwide problem: the same warming that shrinks Alpine ice threatens polar ice sheets and therefore sea levels in coastal cities, including places far from any mountain. It also exposes an awkward trade-off — Switzerland's low-carbon hydropower depends on the very ice that climate change is destroying.

background_read: Switzerland's ice losses are tracked by GLAMOS (a Swiss glacier monitoring network run by universities and supported by the national government), which measures how much snow falls on the glaciers each winter and how much ice melts away each summer. Matthias Huss (a glaciologist who heads GLAMOS) has spent decades measuring and photographing glaciers in the Alps.

The Alps are warming roughly twice as fast as the global average, partly because melting snow and ice reflect less sunlight back into space — a feedback loop scientists call the albedo effect. In 2022, reddish dust blown from the Sahara (the enormous desert across North Africa) settled on the ice and made it absorb extra heat, helping produce that year's record melt as described in the article. The Aletsch Glacier (the largest in the Alps and part of a UNESCO World Heritage site) has been shrinking for more than a century; photographs taken decades apart show its tongue retreating far up the valley.

Because more than half of Switzerland's electricity comes from hydropower and its rivers are fed by glacier melt, the losses matter well beyond scenery and tourism: in a hot, dry summer, less ice means less water for drinking, farming, industry and power.

perspectives.perspective: Climate scientists and monitoring services (positive about the evidence)
perspectives.description: For GLAMOS and the Swiss Academy of Sciences, the value of these measurements is that they remove all doubt: the data show glacier retreat matching exactly what a warming world predicts. Clear, annual numbers make it harder for governments and the public to treat melting ice as a distant or uncertain problem.

The loss is essentially self-inflicted, since Huss attributes the warming entirely to human emissions. The people most affected are not only skiers and tourism businesses but farmers, towns and neighbouring countries that rely on Alpine rivers for drinking water and irrigation.

Alpine glaciers have been retreating since the nineteenth century, but the pace has accelerated sharply since the 1980s. The comparison between 2003 and this year shows something important: percentage losses can grow simply because there is less ice left to lose, so each record year does not require a more extreme heat wave.

Huss argues there is still time to protect the polar ice sheets, where emissions cuts could genuinely limit sea-level rise, even if Alpine glaciers are already committed to shrinking. The open question is speed: whether the world reduces fossil fuel use fast enough for that protection to matter, or whether Switzerland simply has to plan for a future without its glaciers.
